additions.explanation: A single edge whose destination sorts BEFORE its source. The answer is Amsterdam because Zurich has an outgoing edge and Amsterdam does not; alphabetical order has nothing to do with it. Every worked example in the statement happens to have an alphabetically-greatest answer, which is a coincidence of the city names chosen, not a property of the problem.

Two edges listed in reverse path order: A goes to B, B goes to C, so the destination is C. The LAST edge in the list ends at B, which is not the answer, so reading the final pair's destination fails here.
A three-edge chain supplied entirely backwards. The answer D appears as a destination in the FIRST pair and never as a source.

A→B→D→E given out of order. B is both a destination and a source, so any implementation that builds its source set from a slice of the list rather than all of it will mistake B for the end of the line.

Hub appears twice as a source and End twice as a destination: the same city names repeat across pairs. Hub and End each appear exactly twice in the whole list, so counting appearances cannot separate the start from the finish.
A wide fan-out converging on one sink. Hub has three outgoing edges and End has three incoming ones, so the most-mentioned city is ambiguous between the first and the last.
A five-edge chain in path order. Longer than any worked example, so an implementation that inspects only the first pair, or only the first two, has somewhere to go wrong.
Both out of order AND alphabetically inverted: the chain is Zeta → Yale → Xavier, so the answer sorts LAST of the three and appears as a destination in the first pair.
City names that share a prefix and contain a space. "Delhi" is a source and "Delhi Junction" is the destination; nothing may match on prefixes or split on whitespace.
